name: Hair stick / kanzashi / binyeo styling (Asian hairpins)

card.summary: Traditional East Asian ornamental hairpins that hold up buns and topknots and add decorative detail to long hair.
card.note: Pin ends are sharp; use as a hair accessory only.

quick.overview:
Hair sticks are pins used to fasten and decorate hairstyles. The Japanese kanzashi and Korean binyeo are the best-known forms, worn to secure a bun or chignon while adding ornament.

They help appearance by giving long hair a tidy, styled shape and a decorative accent, and historically signalled things like marital status or season. Today they are also worn as a fashion accessory.
quick.how: The pin is typically placed through a twisted bun or topknot to hold it; ornamented types add flowers, beads or carved ends. Kanzashi come as sticks, combs and folded-silk flowers.
quick.risks: Generally low risk as hair accessories. Pin ends are rigid and pointed, and tortoiseshell was historically used.

lead: Kanzashi are traditional Japanese hair ornaments, a term covering hairpins, combs and fabric flowers; in English it usually refers to folded-silk tsumami kanzashi.[1] Binyeo are traditional Korean hairpins used to fix women's chignons and also served as decoration.[2]
Both are used to secure upswept hair and to adorn it. Binyeo marked a married woman and could signal social status; kanzashi use expanded as Edo-period hairstyles grew more elaborate.[1][2]
Today kanzashi appear mainly with geisha, maiko, brides and re-enactors, with ordinary hair clips common; tsumami kanzashi were designated a traditional Tokyo craft in 1982.[1]

chain: Pin secures a bun or topknot
Hair held in a defined shape
angle.text: A hair stick holds up long hair and adds decoration, giving a styled updo without elastics. Ornamented ends serve as accessories.

infobox: Lacquered wood, metal, tortoiseshell, silk, plastic

paras: Kanzashi date to the Jomon period; Chinese hairpins (zan) arrived in the Nara period, kanzashi became a general word for hair ornaments in the Heian period, and Edo-period craftsmanship peaked late.[1] Types include hairpins such as bira-bira, combs (kushi), and tsumami flowers arranged seasonally.[1]

Binyeo trace to the Three Kingdoms era. In Silla, a ban on the wig gache led to binyeo replacing it; Joseon rules restricted gold and silver. They were worn at gyerye coming-of-age, and wooden ones for mourning. Types are the long jam and the U-shaped chae.[2]
No studies found. A 2023 case report describes a hair stick being inserted into a bladder, an unrelated misuse of the object.[3]

timeline.event: Tsumami kanzashi designated a traditional Tokyo craft.[1]
